mainEntity.name: Why has my denture suddenly started hurting after years of being comfortable?

acceptedAnswer.text: A denture that has been comfortable for years may become painful due to gradual changes in the shape of the jawbone beneath it — a natural process called bone resorption. As the ridge changes, the denture may no longer distribute pressure evenly, leading to soreness. Wear to the denture teeth or the acrylic base can also shift how the bite functions. A dental review can determine whether a reline, rebase, or new denture is the most appropriate solution for your specific situation.

mainEntity.name: Can I use denture adhesive to stop the pain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Using denture adhesive may temporarily reduce movement of the denture, but it is not recommended as a solution for a painful or poorly fitting appliance. Adhesive can mask the true extent of the fit problem and may delay you seeking the assessment that is genuinely needed. If you find yourself relying heavily on adhesive to keep your denture in place or to manage discomfort, this is a good indication that your denture requires professional attention.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for gums to shrink under a denture?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is entirely normal for the gum ridge to change shape over time following tooth loss. The jawbone responds to the absence of tooth roots by gradually reducing in volume — a process that continues throughout life. This is why dentures that fitted well at the time of fitting may eventually require adjustment, relining, or replacement. Regular dental reviews help monitor these changes before they cause significant discomfort.

mainEntity.name: What is denture stomatitis and how would I know if I have it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Denture stomatitis is a common condition caused by an overgrowth of the fungus Candida albicans on the tissues beneath the denture. It often appears as redness or mild inflammation of the gum tissue under the denture, and may cause a persistent burning or sore sensation. It is particularly associated with wearing dentures continuously, including overnight, and with inadequate denture hygiene. It is treated with antifungal medication alongside improved cleaning habits and denture removal at night.

mainEntity.name: Should I stop wearing my denture if it is hurting?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally advisable to remove the denture and allow your gum tissue to rest, particularly if significant soreness is present. This can help reduce inflammation before your dental appointment. However, if you need to eat or are in a social situation, wearing it briefly may be unavoidable. If you are removing the denture regularly due to pain, this is a clear sign that a dental assessment is overdue.

mainEntity.name: How often should denture wearers visit the dentist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental professionals advise denture wearers to attend a review at least once a year. This allows your dentist to assess the fit of the appliance, the condition of the denture itself, and the health of your underlying gum tissue. Routine reviews also provide an opportunity for soft tissue screening, which is an important aspect of ongoing oral health monitoring. If you are experiencing any symptoms between scheduled appointments, you should contact your practice without waiting for your next review date.
